title.rendered: Castello del Valentino & Parco del Valentino: Student Guide to PoliTo Architecture Campus

excerpt.rendered: Discover Castello del Valentino, the historic UNESCO World Heritage site housing Politecnico di Torino's Architecture faculty along the Po River in Parco del Valentino.

content.rendered:
Standing majestically on the banks of the Po River, Castello del Valentino is one of Turin's most iconic landmarks and the official campus of Politecnico di Torino's Department of Architecture and Design (DAD).

A UNESCO World Heritage Student Campus

Originally a royal residence of the House of Savoy built in the 17th century, Castello del Valentino was transformed in 1859 into the Royal School of Application for Engineers—the historical predecessor of Politecnico di Torino. Today, international students attend lectures, studio labs, and exhibitions inside this UNESCO-listed castle.

Student Life at Parco del Valentino

Surrounding the castle is Parco del Valentino, Turin's famous riverside park. It is a central hub for student life in Turin:

  • Studying & Outdoor Reading: Shaded lawns and benches right outside lecture halls along the river.
  • Borgo Medievale: The nearby recreated 15th-century medieval village and fortress.
  • Jogging & Cycling: Paved riverside paths connecting Valentino park to San Salvario and Murazzi.
  • ISOT Community Gatherings: Sunset student picnics and weekend gatherings hosted by ISOT Community.

How to Reach Castello del Valentino

  • Metro: Get off at Marconi or Nizza station (Line 1) and walk 5 minutes toward the river.
  • Tram & Bus: GTT Tram lines 9, 16 CD, and 16 CS stop right at Parco del Valentino.
  • Address: Viale Pier Andrea Mattioli 39, 10125 Torino TO.

title.rendered: Turin Public Transport Guide: GTT Student Pass, Metro & Bikesharing

excerpt.rendered: Complete guide to public transit in Turin: GTT annual student subscription discounts (under 26/28), Metro line 1, Night Buster weekend buses, and bike sharing for PoliTo and UniTo students.

content.rendered:
Turin features an efficient, affordable public transportation network operated by GTT (Gruppo Torinese Trasporti), consisting of a driverless underground Metro line, extensive tram and bus routes, and suburban train connections.

GTT Annual Student Pass (Abbonamento Studenti)

Students under 26 (and university students under 28 enrolled at UniTo or PoliTo) qualify for heavily discounted annual transit passes valid for 12 consecutive months across the entire Formula U (Urban City Zone) network.

Student Pass Rates & Options

  • Formula U Annual Student Pass (Under 26/28): ~€258/year (unlimited trips on all buses, trams, and Metro).
  • ISEE Income Reductions: Students residing in Piedmont with low ISEE scores can get further reduced rates (as low as €158/year).

How to Get Your BIP Smart Card & Pass

1. Request a BIP Card (Smart Card): Order your BIP card online via the GTT e-commerce portal or through your university portal (UniTo Smart Card / PoliTo Student ID card).
2. Buy your Pass Online: Log into gtt.to.it or use the TO Move app on Android/iOS.
3. Activate on First Ride: Tap your BIP card or smartphone against the yellow validator upon boarding any bus/tram or entering Metro turnstiles.

Night Buster (Weekend Night Buses)

For late-night weekend trips, GTT operates the Night Buster network every Friday, Saturday, and eve of holidays from 00:30 to 05:00. Lines converge at Piazza Vittorio Veneto and serve popular student nightlife hubs like San Salvario, Vanchiglia, and Santa Giulia.

Shared Mobility & Bike Sharing

  • RideMovi / ToBike: Stationless electric and classic bike sharing available across Turin with student subscription options.
  • E-Scooters & Car Sharing: Lime, Dott, Voi e-scooters, and Enjoy / ShareNow car sharing.

title.rendered: Healthcare & Tessera Sanitaria in Turin: ASL Registration for International Students

excerpt.rendered: How to register with the Italian National Health Service (SSN) and obtain your Tessera Sanitaria in Turin. ASL offices, voluntary payment details, choosing a general practitioner (Medico di Base), and emergency care.

content.rendered:
Accessing reliable healthcare is vital during your studies in Italy. International students in Turin can register with the Italian National Health Service (Servizio Sanitario Nazionale - SSN) to receive a Tessera Sanitaria (Health Insurance Card) and get assigned a personal general practitioner (Medico di Base).

EU vs Non-EU Students Healthcare

EU / EEA Students

Students from the European Union holding a valid EHIC (European Health Insurance Card) or S1 form are covered for medically necessary treatment in public hospitals and clinics in Turin without extra payment.

Non-EU Students (Voluntary SSN Registration)

Non-EU students can register voluntarily with the SSN for full healthcare rights equivalent to Italian citizens. The voluntary subscription fee covers one calendar year (January 1st to December 31st).

How to Register with ASL in Turin

1. Payment via F24 Slip: Pay the voluntary student contribution fee at any post office or bank using an F24 form (Code 8846 - Region 12 Piemonte).
2. Visit your local ASL Office (ASL Città di Torino):
- ASL Central/Porta Nuova area: Via Vittorio Emanuele II 91
- ASL San Salvario / Nizza area: Via San Secondo 29
- ASL Northern Turin: Corso Toscana 108

Required Documents for ASL Registration

  • Valid Passport & Student Visa
  • Codice Fiscale
  • Permesso di Soggiorno card or official post office receipt (Ricevuta)
  • Proof of enrollment at UniTo, PoliTo, SAA, or ESCP
  • F24 payment receipt
  • Proof of residence (Rental agreement or declaration of hospitality)

Emergency Care & Hospitals in Turin

In case of medical emergencies, dial 112 (Single European Emergency Number). Major public hospitals with 24/7 Emergency Rooms (Pronto Soccorso) in Turin include:

  • Ospedale Molinette (Corso Bramante 88)
  • Ospedale Mauriziano (Largo Filippo Turati 62)
  • Ospedale San Giovanni Bosco (Piazza del Donatore di Sangue 3)

title.rendered: Permesso di Soggiorno in Turin: Complete Student Residence Permit Guide

excerpt.rendered: Complete guide to applying for a Permesso di Soggiorno (Residence Permit) for non-EU international students in Turin: Kit Giallo, post office submission, document checklist, and Questura fingerprint appointment.

content.rendered:
All non-EU international students staying in Italy for more than 90 days must apply for a Permesso di Soggiorno per Motivi di Studio (Residence Permit for Study Purposes) within 8 working days of entering the Schengen area.

Step 1: Pick up the "Kit Giallo" (Postal Kit)

Go to a main branch of Poste Italiane that has a Sportello Amico window (such as the branch near Porta Susa station or Piazza XVIII Dicembre) and ask for a free Kit per il Permesso di Soggiorno (often called the Kit Giallo or Yellow Kit envelope).

Step 2: Required Documents Checklist

  • Modulo 1 (Form 1) completed in black ink.
  • Photocopy of Passport (All pages containing stamps, personal details, and student visa).
  • Proof of Enrollment / Acceptance Letter from Politecnico di Torino, Università di Torino, ESCP, or SAA.
  • Proof of Financial Resources (Bank statement showing min. ~€6,000/year or official scholarship letter from EDISU Piemonte).
  • Proof of Health Insurance (Receipt of voluntary enrollment in SSN Tessera Sanitaria or private insurance policy like W.A.I.).
  • Marca da Bollo (€16.00 duty stamp purchased at any local Tabacchi shop).

Step 3: Post Office Payment & Submission

Bring the unsealed envelope and your original passport to a Sportello Amico window at Poste Italiane:

  • Permesso di Soggiorno Electronic Card Fee: €70.46
  • Postal Service Fee: €30.00
  • Registered Mail (Raccomandata): Paid at the counter.

CRITICAL: Keep the post office receipt (Ricevuta Poste Italiane) safe! This receipt, along with your passport, legally permits you to stay and travel within Italy while waiting for your appointment.

Step 4: Questura Appointment in Turin

The post office will issue an appointment slip (Lettera d'Appuntamento) specifying the date, time, and location for your fingerprinting session (fotosegnalamento) at the Questura di Torino (located at Corso Verona 4 or Via Santa Chiara).

On your appointment day, bring 4 identical passport-sized photos, original documents, and your post office receipt.

Tracking Status

You can track your card status on the official portal: questure.poliziadistato.it/stranieri/ using your 12-digit file number or postal receipt code.

title.rendered: How to Get a Codice Fiscale in Turin: Step-by-Step Guide for International Students

excerpt.rendered: Essential guide to obtaining your Italian tax code (Codice Fiscale) in Turin. Documents needed, Agenzia delle Entrate locations, online booking, and step-by-step instructions for international students.

content.rendered:
Obtaining a Codice Fiscale (Italian Tax Code) is the single most important first step for any international student arriving in Turin. Without a Codice Fiscale, you cannot sign a house rental contract, open an Italian bank account, purchase an annual GTT student bus pass, get an Italian mobile SIM card, or complete your enrollment at Politecnico di Torino or the University of Turin.

What is a Codice Fiscale?

The Codice Fiscale is an alphanumeric code of 16 characters generated based on your full name, gender, date of birth, and country of birth. It is issued free of charge by the Agenzia delle Entrate (Italian Revenue Agency).

Required Documents Checklist

  • Valid Passport or EU National ID Card (Original + 2 printed photocopies of the photo page).
  • Valid Student Visa (for non-EU students) with entry stamp + photocopy of the visa page.
  • Proof of Student Status: Admission letter, enrollment certificate from Universitaly, UniTo, or PoliTo.
  • Completed Form AA4/8 (Domanda di attribuzione codice fiscale) available at the Agenzia delle Entrate office or downloadable online.

Agenzia delle Entrate Offices in Turin

You can apply at any local branch of the Agenzia delle Entrate in Turin:

  • Ufficio Territoriale Torino 1 (City Center / Station): Corso Bolzano 30 (very close to Porta Susa railway station).
  • Ufficio Territoriale Torino 2: Via Rosa 15.
  • Ufficio Territoriale Torino 3: Corso Cosenza 25/A.

How to Apply (2 Methods)

Method A: In-Person Appointment in Turin

1. Book an appointment online using the Agenzia delle Entrate website or app (select "Prenotazione Appuntamenti").
2. Arrive 10 minutes before your scheduled slot with your printed documents.
3. The officer will verify your documents and print your official paper Codice Fiscale certificate on the spot.

Method B: Via the Italian Embassy/Consulate Before Arrival

If you have not yet arrived in Italy, you can request your Codice Fiscale directly through the Italian Embassy or Consulate in your home country during your student visa application process.

Need Community Support?

If you run into issues or need help filling out Form AA4/8, join the ISOT Community Telegram group or visit us at our weekly student meetups in Turin!

It’s recommended to check the university websites or contact their international offices for updated information.

title.rendered: A Complete Guide to Living in Turin for International Students

content.rendered:
Turin, Italy, is a vibrant and historic city that offers a unique experience for international students. From its prestigious universities like the University of Turin and Politecnico di Torino to its rich cultural scene, Turin provides an ideal environment for learning, growth, and social connection.

For international students in Turin, navigating a new city can be exciting yet challenging. This guide covers everything you need to know about student life in Turin, including housing options, university programs, cultural activities, and practical tips for daily living. Whether you’re planning to study for a semester or pursue a full degree, this guide will help you settle in and make the most of your time in this beautiful Italian city.

Turin universities for international students

Turin is home to several prestigious universities and colleges offering programs for international students. Studying in Turin provides access to high-quality education, cultural experiences, and a vibrant student community.

1. University of Turin (Università degli Studi di Torino)

The University of Turin is one of Italy’s oldest and largest universities. It offers a wide range of undergraduate and postgraduate programs for international students, including courses in English. Key benefits include:

  • Wide variety of academic programs
  • International student support services
  • Exchange programs and Erasmus+ opportunities

2. Politecnico di Torino

Politecnico di Torino is renowned for engineering, architecture, and design programs. It attracts students from all over the world and provides specialized support for international students:

  • English-taught degree programs
  • Research opportunities and collaborations with industry
  • Student associations and networking events

3. Scuola di Amministrazione Aziendale (SAA)

SAA in Turin focuses on business, management, and administration courses, offering tailored programs for international students who want to gain professional skills in a global environment:

  • International business programs
  • Workshops and seminars with industry experts
  • Opportunities for internships and networking

4. Other Notable Universities and Colleges in Turin

  • Accademia Albertina di Belle Arti – specializing in fine arts and creative studies.
  • ESCP Business School – Turin Campus – offering international business and management programs.
  • International University College of Turin (IUC Turin) – focusing on law, economics, and social sciences.
  • LINK Campus University – Turin Programs – international programs in governance and communications.
  • Other specialized schools and institutes for arts, business, and technology

5. Tips for International Students

  • Check the language of instruction and consider language courses if necessary.
  • Explore scholarship opportunities for international students.
  • Join student clubs and associations to meet fellow students and integrate into the community.
  • Contact the university’s international office for guidance on housing, visas, and student services.

Choosing the right university or college in Turin is a crucial step for any international student in Turin, ensuring a rewarding academic experience and a smooth integration into Italian student life. If you want to see the full list of universities and colleges, visit the page Universities and Colleges in Turin for International Students.

Housing for international students Turin

1. University Dormitories

Many universities, such as the University of Turin and Politecnico di Torino, offer on-campus or affiliated dormitories. Dormitories are a convenient and affordable choice, providing:

  • Shared or private rooms
  • Access to common facilities such as kitchens and lounges
  • Opportunities to meet fellow international students

2. Private Apartments

Renting a private apartment gives more independence and privacy. Popular areas for students include:

  • Centro (City Center) – close to universities and public transport
  • Crocetta – quiet residential area popular with students
  • San Salvario – lively neighborhood with cafes, restaurants, and nightlife

Monthly rent can vary from €350 to €700 depending on location and apartment size.

3. Shared Apartments (Flatshares)

Sharing an apartment with other students is a common and cost-effective option. Benefits include:

  • Lower rent compared to private apartments
  • Opportunities to build friendships with other students
  • Shared utilities and household responsibilities

4. Tips for Finding Accommodation

  • Start searching early, especially before the semester begins.
  • Use trusted platforms like University Housing Services or local student groups.
  • Visit the property in person or request a virtual tour to avoid scams.
  • Check the lease terms carefully, including deposits and utility costs.

Choosing the right accommodation can significantly enhance your experience as an international student in Turin, helping you settle in comfortably and focus on your studies and social life.

Student life in Turin

Turin offers a vibrant and engaging environment for international students. From cultural events to student clubs and social activities, student life in Turin provides numerous opportunities to connect, learn, and enjoy your time in Italy.

1. Cultural Activities and Events

Turin hosts a variety of cultural events throughout the year, including art exhibitions, music festivals, and food fairs. These events are excellent opportunities for international students to:

  • Experience Italian culture and traditions
  • Meet other students from around the world
  • Participate in community activities and workshops

2. Student Clubs and Associations

Universities in Turin have numerous clubs and student associations, which can help you build friendships, develop skills, and participate in extracurricular activities:

  • Language exchange groups
  • Sports clubs and fitness activities
  • Academic and professional societies

3. Networking and Career Opportunities

Being an international student in Turin also provides opportunities to network and enhance your career prospects:

  • Workshops, seminars, and career fairs
  • Internships with local and international companies
  • Professional networking events organized by universities and student associations

4. Social Life and Leisure

Turin has a lively social scene, with cafes, restaurants, bars, and outdoor spaces where students can relax and socialize. Popular student-friendly areas include:

  • San Salvario – for nightlife and social gatherings
  • Crocetta – quiet, residential area popular with students
  • City Center (Centro) – cultural hubs, libraries, and shopping

Engaging in student life in Turin will not only enrich your educational experience but also help you build lasting friendships and integrate smoothly into the international student community.

Transportation and Getting Around

Getting around Turin is easy and convenient for international students. The city offers a variety of transportation options, from public transit to cycling, allowing students to explore the city and commute to university efficiently.

1. Public Transportation

  • Discounted student passes for monthly or yearly travel
  • Easy access to universities, shopping areas, and cultural sites
  • Real-time updates through the official transport app (GTT Torino)

2. Biking and Walking

Turin is a bike-friendly city, and many students prefer cycling or walking for short distances:

  • Public bike-sharing programs available throughout the city
  • Safe bike lanes connecting major areas and universities
  • Walking is a convenient option in the city center (Centro)

3. Trains and Regional Travel

For trips outside Turin, the train network is fast and reliable:

  • High-speed trains to major Italian cities like Milan, Florence, and Rome
  • Regional trains for nearby towns and scenic destinations
  • Student discounts available on some train tickets

4. Tips for International Students

  • Get a student transport card as soon as you arrive to save on daily commuting costs.
  • Plan your route using mobile apps like Google Maps or Moovit for real-time directions.

  • Consider walking or cycling for health benefits and to explore hidden parts of the city.

Living and studying in Turin can be exciting, but it’s important for international students to know the resources and tips that make life easier, affordable, and enjoyable. Being part of the ISOT Community can also help you connect with fellow international students and access local support.

1. Transportation Tips

  • Use apps like GTT Torino, Google Maps, or Moovit to check routes and schedules in real time.

2. Housing and Financial Aid

  • Start searching for housing early to secure the best dormitories or private apartments.
  • Consider shared apartments to lower rent and meet other students.

3. Academic and Career Resources

  • Make use of university libraries, study rooms, and online databases for research and study support.
  • Participate in workshops, seminars, and career fairs offered by your university to boost skills and networking.

4. Social and Cultural Resources

  • Join student clubs, language exchange groups, and cultural associations to meet new friends and integrate into the community.
  • Take advantage of events, festivals, and cultural tours organized by the universities, local organizations, and ISOT Community.
  • Use online platforms and social media groups for international students to stay updated on events and opportunities.

By utilizing these tips, resources, and the support of the ISOT Community, international students in Turin can enjoy a smoother transition, save money, and make the most of their study experience in the city.

Conclusion

Living in Turin as an international student can be an enriching and exciting experience. From top universities like the University of Turin and Politecnico di Torino, to affordable housing options, cultural events, and a vibrant student community, the city offers everything needed for academic and personal growth. By taking advantage of resources such as student transport cards, ADiSU scholarships, and the support of the ISOT Community, international students in Turin can make the most of their time, build lasting friendships, and thrive in a new environment.

1. Are there English-taught programs in Turin universities?

Yes, universities such as Politecnico di Torino and the University of Turin offer several programs in English, especially at the master’s level. Always check the university website for up-to-date course offerings for international students.

Students under 26 years old can use public transportation cards for free, including buses, trams, and metro services. Make sure to register for your student card at the beginning of your semester.

Yes, students with ADiSU scholarships can get free or subsidized university accommodation. Additionally, ISOT Community can provide guidance on finding verified housing options and shared apartments.

Joining student clubs, cultural associations, and events organized by your university or the ISOT Community is the best way to meet fellow international students, practice languages, and make friends.

title.rendered: Happy Nowruz, Iranian New Year: ISOT Community

content.rendered:
As the arrival of spring marks the beginning of a new year, ISOT Community extends its warmest wishes to all celebrating Nowruz—the ancient Persian festival of renewal, hope, and togetherness. This joyous occasion, which has been celebrated for over 3,000 years, symbolizes rebirth, unity, and the triumph of light over darkness.

The Spirit of Nowruz

Nowruz, meaning “New Day” in Persian, is more than just a calendar event. It is a time for reflection, gratitude, and new beginnings. It reminds us to embrace growth, positivity, and cultural heritage, strengthening the bonds that unite us.

At the heart of Nowruz is the Haft-Seen table, a traditional display of seven symbolic items, each representing prosperity, health, and renewal:

✔ Sabzeh (sprouted greens) – Rebirth and growth
✔ Samanu (sweet pudding) – Strength and patience
✔ Senjed (dried lotus fruit) – Love and wisdom
✔ Seer (garlic) – Protection and health
✔ Seeb (apple) – Beauty and vitality
✔ Somāq (sumac) – The color of sunrise, symbolizing a new beginning
✔ Serkeh (vinegar) – Patience and wisdom

🔥 Traditions That Bring Us Together

Before Nowruz, families gather for Chaharshanbe Suri, a fire-jumping festival symbolizing purification and letting go of negativity. As we leap over the flames, we say, “Zardi-ye man az to, sorkhi-ye to az man!” (May my weakness be yours, and your strength be mine).

Another cherished tradition is Sizdah Bedar, celebrated on the 13th day of Nowruz, where people head outdoors for a picnic, embracing nature and wishing for a bright year ahead.

💙 A Message of Unity

As an international student community, ISOT takes pride in celebrating diverse cultures and traditions. Nowruz is a time to strengthen friendships, embrace new opportunities, and spread kindness. No matter where we are, this festival reminds us that renewal and hope transcend borders.

 

May this Nowruz bring peace, success, and happiness to you and your loved ones. Let’s welcome the new year with open hearts and a spirit of togetherness!

Happy Nowurz and New YEAR

 

ISOT Community Board Members

title.rendered: Student Housing in Turin: A Complete Guide

content.rendered:
How to Find Student Housing in Turin: A Complete Guide

Turin, a vibrant student city, is home to thousands of international students studying at institutions like Politecnico di Torino and Università degli Studi di Torino. Finding the right housing is crucial for a comfortable and productive academic life. This guide will walk you through the best options, costs, and essential tips for securing student accommodation in Turin.

1. Types of Student Accommodation

a) University Dormitories

Both Politecnico di Torino and Università di Torino offer student dormitories through organizations like EDISU Piemonte. These accommodations are affordable and often include utilities, Wi-Fi, and communal areas.

  • Pros: Affordable, social environment, close to university campuses.

  • Cons: Limited availability, application process required.

  • How to apply: Check the EDISU website (www.edisu.piemonte.it) and apply early.

b) Private Student Residences

If you prefer a more modern and comfortable setting, private student residences are a great option. Some popular ones include:

  • CX Turin (CampusX)

  • Aparto Student Turin

  • Camplus These residences offer amenities like gyms, study rooms, and social events but come at a higher price.

  • Pros: Fully furnished, modern, student-friendly services.

  • Cons: More expensive than university dorms.

c) Shared Apartments (“Appartamenti in condivisione”)

Many students choose to rent a private apartment and share it with roommates. Websites and Facebook groups help find available rooms.

  • Pros: More independence, flexible options.

  • Cons: Utility costs may not be included, longer searching process.

  • Best Websites:

    • Idealista (www.idealista.it)

    • Bakeca (www.bakeca.it)

    • Uniaffitti (www.uniaffitti.it)

    • Facebook Groups (e.g., “Affitti studenti Torino”)

d) Homestays (Living with an Italian Family)

For those who want to improve their Italian and experience local culture, a homestay with an Italian family can be an option.

  • Pros: Cultural immersion, meals often included.

  • Cons: Less privacy, house rules may apply.

  • Where to find: Websites like Homestay.com and local Facebook groups.

2. Average Rent Prices in Turin

Prices vary depending on location and accommodation type. Here’s a general overview:

  • University Dorms: €250–€400/month

  • Shared Apartments: €300–€500/month per room

  • Private Studios: €500–€800/month

  • Private Student Residences: €500–€900/month

Additional costs such as utilities (€50–€100/month) and internet (€20–€30/month) should be considered.

3. Best Neighborhoods for Students

Choosing the right area is essential for a good living experience. Here are some of the best student-friendly neighborhoods:

  • San Salvario – Lively area with bars and restaurants, close to the city center.

  • Vanchiglia – Artistic and youthful, near Università di Torino.

  • San Donato – Affordable and well-connected to public transport.

  • Cenisia – Near Politecnico di Torino, popular with students.

  • Lingotto – Cheaper rents, good metro access.

4. How to Secure an Apartment in Turin

Step 1: Start Early

Finding housing in Turin can be competitive, especially before the academic year begins. Start searching at least 2–3 months before arrival.

Step 2: Use Reliable Platforms

Avoid scams by using trusted websites like Idealista, Bakeca, and EDISU. Always visit the apartment in person or request a video tour before making any payment.

Step 3: Prepare Necessary Documents

Landlords may require the following:

  • Passport or residence permit

  • Proof of university enrollment

  • Guarantor details (if applicable)

  • One or two months’ rent as a deposit

Step 4: Sign a Contract

Ensure you get a written contract (“contratto di locazione”) that specifies:

  • Rent amount and included expenses

  • Deposit terms

  • Duration of the contract

  • House rules (if any)

5. Tips to Avoid Scams

  • Never send money upfront without verifying the property and landlord.

  • Check for official registration (ask for a “codice fiscale” and contract).

  • Avoid unrealistic offers (too cheap compared to average market prices).

  • Use official rental agencies for added security.

6. Conclusion

Finding student housing in Turin requires planning and research, but with the right approach, you can secure a comfortable and affordable place. Whether you choose university dorms, shared apartments, or private residences, be sure to start early, use trusted resources, and always verify before committing. Good luck with your search, and enjoy your student life in Turin!

  • Bakeca: www.bakeca.it

title.rendered: Understanding the Italian University Exam System

content.rendered:
Introduction

Italy is home to some of the oldest and most prestigious universities in the world, attracting students from all over the globe. If you’re studying in Italy, understanding how exams work is essential to navigating your academic journey. The Italian university exam system has unique features that may differ from what you’re used to in your home country.

Types of Exams

In Italian universities, exams can take different forms depending on the course and professor’s preference:

  1. Oral Exams (“Esami Orali”) – A traditional and widely used method where students discuss topics with a professor. This exam tests not only knowledge but also reasoning and communication skills.

  2. Written Exams (“Esami Scritto”) – These can include multiple-choice questions, essays, problem-solving exercises, or a mix of formats.

  3. Practical Exams – Common in scientific and technical courses, students must complete a task or project to demonstrate their skills.

Grading System

Exams in Italy are graded on a 30-point scale, with 18/30 being the minimum passing grade. If you perform exceptionally well, you may receive 30 e Lode (30 with honors), the highest possible grade. Final degree classifications are based on a 110-point scale, where 110 e Lode is the maximum score.

Exam Sessions

Italian universities typically have two or three main exam sessions per academic year:

  • Winter session (January-February)

  • Summer session (June-July)

  • Autumn session (September)

Students can often choose when to take an exam, as multiple dates (called “appelli”) are offered per session. This flexibility allows students to prepare at their own pace.

Retaking Exams

One of the advantages of the Italian system is that students can retake exams if they fail or wish to improve their grade. However, policies vary by university and professor, so it’s important to check specific rules.

Registration and Exam Rules

  • Students must register for exams in advance through the university’s online system.

  • During oral exams, students are usually examined one by one, sometimes in front of other students.

  • Professors can sometimes allow students to refuse a grade if they are not satisfied and retake the exam in a later session.

title.rendered: Celebrating Migration: A Journey of Resilience and Opportunity

content.rendered:
As the world observes International Migrants Day on December 18, I find myself reflecting on the profound impact of migration—not just globally, but also in my own life and the stories I’ve encountered. Migration is not just about movement; it’s about people’s courage, their ability to adapt, and the opportunities they create. For me, and for ISOT, an organization built on fostering inclusivity and celebrating diversity, this day is deeply personal and profoundly meaningful.

Migration has been part of humanity’s story since the beginning of time. Across centuries, people have moved in search of safety, opportunity, and better lives. Whether driven by conflict, economic hardship, or the innate desire to explore, every migrant’s journey is one of courage and transformation. These stories resonate with me because they are about hope, resilience, and the universal dreams we all share.

Today, migration continues to shape societies in powerful ways. It brings vibrancy to our communities, enriches cultures, and fosters innovation. Recent developments in the Middle East, particularly the ongoing struggles in Syria, highlight not just the challenges faced by migrants but also their hope and determination. The traffic of migrants returning from Turkey to Syria, for example, underscores a growing desire to rebuild their lives in their homeland despite ongoing challenges. This sentiment reminds us all of our shared responsibility to create a safer, more stable world. Safety, dignity, and opportunity should never be luxuries—they should be fundamental rights for everyone.

Here in Europe, local organizations like ISOT play a vital role in creating inclusive and diverse communities. These organizations don’t just support migrants—they provide pathways for integration and help unlock the potential of newcomers. For instance, they often guide international students and professionals through challenges like adapting to local hiring processes or navigating complex legal regulations. Many migrants face barriers such as a lack of knowledge about rules and workplace expectations, which can hinder their ability to fully participate in the economy. By addressing these issues, organizations like ISOT ensure that migration is not a burden but a tremendous opportunity. This inclusivity enriches Europe by leveraging diverse skills and perspectives, ultimately driving social cohesion and economic growth.

I’ve often thought about how local organizations can also be tools for European entities to create opportunities that are more equitable for non-native citizens. When migrants are empowered to participate fully in the economy, they bring fresh ideas and new energy that can spark innovation. This process isn’t just about helping migrants—it’s about recognizing their contributions and using their talents to drive meaningful change in our societies. Migration, when embraced with openness, can be a source of creativity and transformation for developed countries.

I’m constantly inspired by the resilience of migrants who adapt to new environments while holding onto their cultural roots. It’s a delicate balance—blending the past with the present—that showcases incredible strength and adaptability. But this journey isn’t without its challenges: language barriers, cultural misunderstandings, and the sense of being caught between two worlds. That’s why creating inclusive spaces where migrants feel valued and supported is so important.

One area that fascinates me is the process of cultural adaptation, especially for those from multicultural backgrounds. It’s a journey that reveals the beauty and complexity of living between worlds. Through my research, I’ve come to understand how migrants don’t just adapt—they contribute. They spark global conversations about diversity, inclusivity, and the richness of human experience. Their stories offer lessons on how we can build societies that celebrate differences instead of fearing them.

On this International Migrants Day, I believe we all have a responsibility to reflect on how we can do better. Are we giving migrants a voice? Are we creating spaces where they feel included? Are we fully recognizing and appreciating their contributions? These questions matter because they challenge us to ensure migration remains a story of hope and opportunity—for everyone.

In celebrating this day, let’s honor the courage of those who embark on these life-changing journeys. Let’s also commit to building a world where everyone—regardless of their origin—can thrive. Together, with organizations like ISOT leading the way, we can turn migration into a transformative force for good, one that brings innovation, equity, and hope to the world.

The situation for 2024/25 scholarships is critical:

🔴 Delays in Payments: No first installments until February due to liquidity issues, despite the Ministry’s request to anticipate payments.

UPDATE: DEC 11th

FINAL DATA ON COVERAGE AND PAYMENT OF FIRST INSTALLMENTS OF EDISU

Following the Board of Directors meeting on December 10th, we are posting this update with more precise information regarding the coverage and disbursement of the first installments we mentioned in our previous post.

COVERAGE: As of 5:00 PM on 10/12, there are 18,572 students who meet the requirements to win the scholarship, and 80 applications are still being evaluated. The total need amounts to approximately €102 million. In addition to this figure, €1 million must be added for doctoral scholarships, as well as the need for funds to cover 1,700 suspended students who will be evaluated in the April rankings.

In total, EDISU currently has €88.8 million. Yesterday, EDISU received a formal commitment letter for €27 million from President of the Region Cirio, Vice President Chiorino, and Budget Assessor Tronzano. However, this letter may not mean much unless the Regional Council or the Regional Government approve the 2025 budget with the allocation for EDISU. Therefore, as of now, EDISU cannot rely on these funds.

IMPORTANT: After more precise calculations, €6 million of the €88.8 million must be deducted (to cover Graduation Awards, Part-Time Collaborations, etc.), along with another €6.4 million that was already allocated for the November rankings for first-year undergraduate and single-cycle master’s students. Thus, approximately 25% of eligible students will not receive the funds. It’s important to note that in the fund distribution, only 15% is reserved for first-year students, so it’s likely that the percentage of eligible students will be higher in the first years compared to later years.

FIRST INSTALLMENT PAYMENTS: We raised the issue in the Board of Directors regarding EDISU’s cash flow and the payment of the first installments. The offices informed us that the current cash flow will only allow for the payment of the first installment to the first-year students who won the November rankings (those who received the 20% advance on their first installment at the end of November and will receive the remaining 30% balance in December). We also inquired about the monetization of the accommodation spots for the Universiade, and were told that the offices are working to disburse the monetization starting next week (pending resolution of some accounting issues and payment application bugs). It is not guaranteed that the monetizations will be paid by December, but we will request updates.

Lastly, we confirmed that all second installments have been paid and that cash flow issues have not affected their payment. We were assured that all payments have been processed and that everyone should have received the second installment for the 2023/24 academic year. If this is not the case for you, please open a support ticket to investigate your specific situation.

To build a collective movement in support of our RIGHT TO EDUCATION and to discuss the current situation at EDISU, we remind you of the Assembly on Friday, December 13th at 5:30 PM at the Olimpia canteen.

title.rendered: Sexual Behaviour in Italy

content.rendered:
Sexual Education and Its Importance

Sexual education is a vital part of personal awareness, helping individuals build safe, healthy, and informed relationships. It covers topics such as understanding the body, preventing sexually transmitted diseases, hygiene, emotional relationships, and the importance of consent. This knowledge supports both physical and mental well-being.

Education in this area promotes growth, improves quality of life, and prevents potential risks.

A) The Concept of Consent

Consent in sexual relationships means an informed, voluntary, and mutual agreement to engage in any sexual activity. Consent must be clear, specific, and reversible. If one party feels uncomfortable or says “no,” the other party must respect this decision. Informed Consent: Both parties fully understand the situation, and the decision is based on complete information.

Voluntary Consent: There should be no coercion, threat, or psychological pressure influencing the decision.

B) Healthy Relationships

Healthy relationships are based on mutual respect, trust, and honest communication. In

such relationships:

Both parties care about each other’s needs and feelings. Problems are solved through respectful communication, not violence or disrespect. Emotional and psychological support is present.

C) Types of Sexual Orientation Sexual orientation refers to the emotional or sexual attraction a person has toward a specific gender or genders. These include:

Heterosexual: Attraction to the opposite gender.

Homosexual: Attraction to the same gender.

Bisexual: Attraction to both genders.

Asexual: Lack of sexual or romantic attraction.

Respecting others’ sexual orientations and accepting differences are essential principles in a healthy society.

title.rendered: Useful Medical Instruction for Students

content.rendered:
In Italy, emergency medical services at public hospitals are free and available to everyone, even without a health card. For non-emergency care, services can be accessed through the ASL (local health authority), but some may require a Tessera Sanitaria or involve costs. Essential care is often provided regardless of insurance or residency status. Contact ASL for details on available services and requirements.

Free HPV Vaccination in Turin

In Italy, the HPV (Human Papillomavirus) vaccine is a significant preventive measure to reduce cervical cancer risk. This vaccine is free for certain populations, including adolescent girls and young women aged 11 to 29. The Italian government has implemented free vaccination programs nationwide to promote public health and prevent  disease spread.

In Turin, various health and medical centers provide free HPV vaccination. These centers, under the ASL (Azienda Sanitaria Locale) framework, offer services free of charge or at low cost to students and residents of the area.

Who We Are

We are ISOT — an international student community based in the vibrant city of Turin. Our community is a space where people from all cultures, languages, and backgrounds come together to feel seen, supported, and empowered. We believe in the power of connection — not just socially, but emotionally and intellectually. What makes ISOT special isn’t just what we do — it’s how we do it: with heart, openness, and a shared belief that diversity makes us stronger. Here, you’re not just a student. We listen to the needs of international students and respond with real, practical solutions — from organizing cultural events and support sessions, to creating spaces where people feel safe, seen, and inspired.
